J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. This appeal is directed against the order dated 27th November,
2015 passed by 1st Respondent, Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the Commission”) thereby
approving the transmission tariff for Vallur TPS-Melakottaiyur 400
kV D/C line under supplementary Transmission system associated
with Vallur TPS in Southern Region from its Commercial Operation
Date (COD) to 31st March, 2014 for the tariff block 2009-14, in
terms of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and
Conditions) of Tariff Regulations, 2009 (hereinafter referred to “the
2009 Tariff Regulations”).
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 3 of 25

2. The 2nd Respondent – Power Grid Corporation of India Limited
(PGCIL) had filed the petition No. 48/TT/2013 seeking approval of
the transmission tariff for its above mentioned transmission asset
from its COD till 31st March, 2014.
3. The Appellant has assailed the said tariff order in this appeal
with following three grounds:-
i. The quantity variation allowed by the Commission is
unjustified, being based on vague reasons such as
urbanization and route deviation without any supporting
material;
ii. The claim of price variation made by 2nd Respondent as
allowed by the Commission in the impugned order is
contrary to competitive bidding principles and inconsistent
with the indices published by the Indian Electrical and
Electronics Manufacturers’ Association (IEEMA); and
iii. Incidental Expenses during Construction (IEDC) ought not
to have been allowed by the Commission as there is no
provision for the same in the 2009 Regulations.
iv. The impugned order is devoid of any reasoning.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 4 of 25

4. We have heard Mr. S. Vallinayagam, Learned Counsel for the
Appellant and Mr. Shubham Arya, learned Counsel for 2nd
Respondent. None of the other respondents have contested the
appeal. We have also gone through the written submissions filed by
the Learned Counsels.
5. Issue wise submissions made by the Learned Counsels are
noted hereunder :-
Issue (i) – Quantity Variation
6. It is argued by the Learned Counsel for the Appellant that 2nd
Respondent has not given any justification supported by
documentary proof to substantiate its contention that there was
variation in the quantity of goods procured for completion of the
asset. He further pointed out that the 2nd Respondent had not made
any mention of Right of Way (RoW) issue anywhere in the petition
including form 5(B). It is also his submission that the Commission
has not given any reason for accepting the contention of the 2nd
Respondent that rapid urbanization was responsible for increase in
number of towers.
7. Per contra, it is argued on behalf of the 2nd Respondent that the
quantity as reflected in the feasibility report is derived on the basis
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 5 of 25

of the preliminary/walk-over survey which is only indicative and
intended for broad cost estimation at the planning stage. It is
submitted that such estimates are inherently tentative and subject to
revision upon undertaking detailed survey, profiling, and soil
investigation during the execution phase of the project. On this
aspect reliance is placed upon the judgement of this Tribunal dated
30th May, 2023 in Appeal No. 172 of 2023 in Baitarani Power Project
Private Limited vs. OERC & Ors.
8. It is argued that as per the Central Board of Irrigation and
Power, Manual on Transmission Lines, a minimum of Right of Way
(RoW) of about 46 meters is required for a 400 kV D/C line and
where such unit is not available due to field constraints, change of
alignment is necessary, leading to increase in towers and
associated works. It is argued that issues related to RoW should not
have been identified at the walk-over stage, and therefore, variation
in quantities on account of the same becomes an uncontrollable
factor. Learned Counsel further argued that the increase in the
project cost from Rs.46.38 crores (as per FR) to Rs.58.71 crores
resulting in a variation of 12.35 crores has been duly explained by
the 2nd Respondent before the Commission as attributable to
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 6 of 25

quantity variation and price variation. It is submitted that variation in
quantities is a well recognized and inherent feature of infrastructure
in transmission projects and under Regulation 7 & 9 of 2009 Tariff
Regulations, the Commission was only required to undertake
prudence check of the captive cost based on the actual expenditure
incurred which has been done by the Commission in the instant case
before approving the claim of the 2nd Respondent. Thus, it is argued
that the increase in quantities is solely attributable to actual project
requirements, route alignments, constraints, rapid urbanization,
increase in angle towers, foundation requirements, tower steel,
insulators and other associated works which aspects were duly
examined by the Commission.
Issue (ii) - Price Variation
9. Learned Counsel for the Appellant pointed out that the cost of
the transmission asset as stated by the 2nd Respondent in Feasibility
Report (FR) was Rs.46.38 crores whereas its completion cost has
been claimed as Rs.58.71 crores, there being increase on
approximately 26.58% in the capital cost. He argued that to
substantiate such price variation, the 2nd Respondent did not furnish
any details of the contracts entered into by it with various
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 7 of 25

contractors. It is submitted that there is no explanation as to how the
price levels of awarded packages could change after a successful
bidder is selected. It is further argued that the 2nd Respondent did
not provide the start and ends dates of the supply contracts as well
as applicable WPI (month-wise). Learned Counsel further argued
that there cannot be any price variation in a project awarded in
pursuance to competitive bidding. According to the Learned
Counsel, the Commission has wrongly allowed the claimed 26%
increase in the capital cost of the project without assigning any
reason and even after noting that the 2nd Respondent has been
casual in calculating the FR cost.
10. Per contra, Learned Counsel for 2nd Respondent submitted
that the price variation has happened as a natural consequence of
market fluctuations during the execution of the project on account of
inherent time gap between the submission of the physical report and
procurement of key inputs such as steel, cement, and aluminum etc.
It is argued that the contracts entered into by the 2nd Respondent
contain specific clauses related to price variation/escalation which
are standard in the nature, to account for fluctuations in prices.
According to the Learned Counsel, price variation has been
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 8 of 25

computed strictly in accordance with the applicable formula and
indices prescribed under the contract including the indices published
by the Indian Electrical & Electronics Manufacturers' Association
(IEEMA). He argued that the price variation is well recognised and
integral component of cost plus tariff determination particularly in
context of regulated transmission projects. He submitted that the
details of price variation including application of indices and
computation methodology were placed before the Central
Commission which have been examined during the process of
prudence check and the Commission has allowed the price variation
as part of the admitted capital cost only upon being satisfied that
the escalation is in accordance with the contractual provisions and
reflects actual market conditions. Learned Counsel placed reliance
upon the previous judgement of this Tribunal dated 12th September,
2025 in Appeal No. 259 of 2018 in the matter of Manchukonda
Agrotech Pvt. Ltd. Vs. KERC & Anr. in which it has been held as
under :-
“67. In a project-specific tariff determination, the State
Commission is bound to consider the actual cost data
supported by genuine invoices and then to determine the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 9 of 25

final cost after a prudent check. It cannot adopt a figure that
is submitted as an estimated figure part of the DPR, as
against the actual/realistic cost data.”
Issue (iii) – IEDC
11. Learned Counsel for the Appellant submitted that there is no
provision for IEDC (Incidental Expenses During Construction) in
Tariff Regulations, 2009 and, therefore, the Commission ought not
to have allowed the same. He further submitted that 2nd Respondent
had not made any claim for IEDC in the tariff petition and had merely
mentioned as sum of Rs.4.19 crore under this head in form 5(C) and,
therefore, the Commission has erred in allowing the same.
12. Learned Counsel further submitted that IEDC is a recognized
component of capital cost in transmission tariff determination and
has been allowed by the Commission strictly on the basis of actual
expenditure supported by Auditor’s Certificates.
Issue (iv) – Impugned order being devoid of reasons
13. Learned Counsel for the Appellant would submit that the
Commission, in the impugned order, has only stated that it is
satisfied with the submission of the 2nd Respondent and has failed
to provide any reasons for such satisfaction, as required under law.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 10 of 25

Relying upon the judgement of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in CCT
vs. Shukla & Brothers (2010) 4 SCC 785 wherein the apex court has
underscore the need of proper reasons in a judicial order, Learned
Counsel argued that since the impugned order suffers from lack of
reasoning, the same cannot be sustained and liable to be set aside
outrightly.
14. Learned Counsel for the 2nd Respondent would submit that the
impugned order is a well reasoned order which has been passed by
the Commission upon perusal of entire material placed before it
during the hearing of the petition and does not suffer from any
infirmity on this aspect, as contended on behalf of the Appellant.
Our Analysis :
15. The details of the apportioned approved FR cost and the
capital cost claimed by the 2nd Respondent before the Commission
as on the COD of the asset in question and estimated additional
capital expenditure projected to be incurred for the asset are given
in the following table :-

Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 11 of 25

16. Thus, the 2nd Respondent had submitted the total estimated
completion cost as Rs.5,870.96 lakhs as against the apportioned
approved FR cost of Rs.4,638.00 lakhs, there being cost variation of
26.58%.
17. The Commission, in the impugned order, has noted the scope
of work in paragraph Nos. 3, 4 & 5. The submissions and contentions
raised on behalf of the parties have been noted in paragraph Nos. 9
& 10 of the impugned order. Regulation 7 of 2009 Tariff Regulations
has been extracted in paragraph 12 of the impugned order. The
discussion on “Cost Over Run” starts from paragraph No. 14. The
contentions of Appellant – TANGEDCO on this aspect have been
noted in paragraph 14. The contentions made on behalf of the
Appellant have been noted in paragraph 15, 16 & 17. Thereafter, the
Commission has held and observed in paragraph No. 18 of the
impugned order as under :-
“18. We have considered the submissions of the petitioner
and TANGEDCO. Increase in cost of the instant assets is
due to increase in the quantity of material used and due to
the market conditions. The reasons given by the petitioner
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 12 of 25

for crease in cost is in order and accordingly the cost
increase is allowed. However, the petitioner is directed to
be more diligent while preparing the FR cost.”
18. This is only paragraph in the impugned order in which the
Commission has purportedly returned its findings on the claim of the
2nd Respondent for increase in quantity variation and price variation
leading to 26.58% increase in the capital cost. Indeed there is no
elaborate discussion on the rival contentions/submissions of the
parties, particularly, the objections raised by the Appellant to such
huge variation in the capital cost. The Commission has not bothered
to give reasons for rejecting the objections raised by the Appellant.
In just one sentence, the Commission has observed and concluded
that the reasons given by the 2nd Respondent for increase in cost
are in order and accordingly, allowed the increase in capital cost.
Such an order, by no means, can be termed as a reasoned order.
When we are unable to discern from the impugned order as to what
persuaded the Commission to accept the contentions of the 2nd
Respondent and to reject the contentions of the Appellant, we
cannot expect Appellant to know, upon perusal of the impugned
order, the reason as to why the Commission has held against it.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 13 of 25

19. Further, the Commission has also proceeded to allow IEDC in
the sum of Rs.464.55 lakhs to the 2nd Respondent despite noting
that no details have been furnished by the 2nd Respondent in this
regard and without deliberating upon Regulation 7 of 2009 Tariff
Regulations which do not permit IEDC.
20. We may note that while passing tariff orders, the Commission
exercises quasi judicial functions. Therefore, the Commission is
bound to take note of every suggestions/objections raised before it
by any stake-holder and to give reasons for accepting or rejecting
such suggestions/objections. Reasoned order is the hallmark of
judicial system. A reasoned order provides a clear understanding
of the decision making process and ensures fairness,
accountability and credibility. It reinforces fairness as well as rule
of law and enables effective review/appeal process. It is the
fundamental consideration in decision making process that the
party or the parties must know why and on what grounds the order
has been passed again him/them. A speaking order introduces
fairness in the decision making and helps in minimizing
arbitrariness. The purpose of recording reasons is also to serve
wider aspect of principle of justice that justice must not only be
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 14 of 25

done, it must also seem to be done. Reasons act as a bridge
between the material facts on which conclusion is drawn and the
actual order passed. Reasoning in a judicial order is necessary not
only for the satisfaction of the parties but also for the appellate
court/forum which must know the reasons for arriving at the
decision assailed before it.
21. The Hon’ble Supreme Court has also emphasized in several
cases, the importance of reasoned orders. The requirement of
indicating reasons has been judicially recognized as imperative. In
Raj Kishore Jha Vs. State of Bihar (2003) 11 SCC 519, the Apex
Court held:-
“8. …. Right to reason is an indispensable part of a sound judicial
system; reasons at least sufficient to indicate an application of mind to
the matter before court. Another rationale is that the affected party can
know why the decision has gone against him. One of the salutary
requirements of natural justice is spelling out reasons for the order
made;….”
22. Similarly in Asstt. Commissioner, Commercial Tax Deptt. Vs.
Shukla & Brother (2010) 4 SCC 785, it has been observed as
under:-
“23. We are not venturing to comment upon the correctness or
otherwise of the contentions of law raised before the High Court in the
present petition, but it was certainly expected of the High Court to record
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 15 of 25

some kind of reasons for rejecting the revision petition filed by the
Department at the very threshold. A litigant has a legitimate expectation
of knowing reasons for rejection of his claim/prayer. It is then alone, that
a party would be in a position to challenge the order on appropriate
grounds. Besides, this would be for the benefit of the higher or the
appellate court. As arguments bring things hidden and obscure to the
light of reasons, reasoned judgment where the law and factual matrix of
the case is discussed, provides lucidity and foundation for conclusions
or exercise of judicial discretion by the courts.
24. Reason is the very life of law. When the reason of a law once ceases,
the law itself generally ceases (Wharton's Law Lexicon). Such is the
significance of reasoning in any rule of law. Giving reasons furthers the
cause of justice as well as avoids uncertainty. As a matter of fact it helps
in the observance of law of precedent. Absence of reasons on the
contrary essentially introduces an element of uncertainty, dissatisfaction
and give entirely different dimensions to the questions of law raised
before the higher/appellate courts. In our view, the court should provide
its own grounds and reasons for rejecting claim/prayer of a party
whether at the very threshold i.e. at admission stage or after regular
hearing, howsoever concise they may be.
25. We would reiterate the principle that when reasons are announced
and can be weighed, the public can have assurance that process of
correction is in place and working. It is the requirement of law that
correction process of judgments should not only appear to be
implemented but also seem to have been properly implemented.
Reasons for an order would ensure and enhance public confidence and
would provide due satisfaction to the consumer of justice under our
justice dispensation system. It may not be very correct in law to say, that
there is a qualified duty imposed upon the Courts to record reasons.
26. Our procedural law and the established practice, in fact, imposes
unqualified obligation upon the courts to record reasons. There is hardly
any statutory provision under the Income Tax Act or under the
Constitution itself requiring recording of reasons in the judgments but it
is no more res integra and stands unequivocally settled by different
judgments of this Court holding that the courts and tribunals are required
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 16 of 25

to pass reasoned judgments/orders. In fact, Order 14 Rule 2 read
with Order 20 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires that, the
Court should record findings on each issue and such findings which
obviously should be reasoned would form part of the judgment, which in
turn would be the basis for writing a decree of the Court.
27. By practice adopted in all Courts and by virtue of judge-made law,
the concept of reasoned judgment has become an indispensable part of
basic rule of law and, in fact, is a mandatory requirement of the
procedural law. Clarity of thoughts leads to clarity of vision and proper
reasoning is the foundation of a just and fair decision. In Alexander
Machinery (Dudley) Ltd. there are apt observations in this regard to say
"failure to give reasons amounts to denial of justice". Reasons are the
real live links to the administration of justice. With respect we will
contribute to this view. There is a rationale, logic and purpose behind a
reasoned judgment. A reasoned judgment is primarily written to clarify
own thoughts; communicate the reasons for the decision to the
concerned and to provide and ensure that such reasons can be
appropriately considered by the appellate/higher court. Absence of
reasons thus would lead to frustrate the very object stated hereinabove.”
23. Thus, reason is the heartbeat of every conclusion and without
the same, it becomes lifeless. Giving reason furthers the cause of
justice and avoids arbitrariness as well as uncertainty. A litigant has
a legitimate expectations of knowing the reasons for rejection of his
claim/prayer.
24. Having held that the impugned order of the Commission is
bereft of reasons, we also take note of the fact that the Tariff
determination under the regulatory framework is a continuous and
iterative process, wherein each order of the Commission is subject
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 17 of 25

to subsequent true-up and re-determination exercises in each
control period. The order Impugned in this Appeal is passed in
November 2016 pertains to tariff determination for the concerned
assets in tariff Block 2009-14, subsequent to COD of the Asset. It
is evident that true up for said Assets as well as tariff determination
for the subsequent tariff blocks must have been carried out and
tariff paid by the beneficiaries in terms of those later orders. We
are, however, not been appraised about the status of subsequent
tariff orders passed in respect of the subject assets, however, the
inevitable consequence is that findings in this order stand eclipsed
by later tariff re-determinations which, if not challenged, would have
attained finality.
25. Ordinarily, an order lacking adequate reasoning would merit
remand. However, in the circumstances of the present case as
noted above, such a course may be futile, as the regulatory
trajectory has already advanced through subsequent orders. It is
trite that the Appellate Tribunal, while exercising jurisdiction under
Section 111 of the Electricity Act, 2003, is not constrained merely
by the form or sufficiency of reasoning in the order impugned before
it. The absence of elaborate reasons does not denude this Tribunal
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 18 of 25

of the power to adjudicate the controversy on merits. Being the first
appellate forum, the Tribunal is vested with plenary authority to
examine the legality, propriety, and correctness of the order under
challenge, and to render findings based on the statutory framework,
regulatory principles, and the material placed on record.
26. Considering the above noted facts & circumstances, we are
of the view that no useful purpose will be achieved in remanding
the case back to the Commission for a fresh consideration. It will
be only an academic exercise as the entire material is before us in
this appeal which we can peruse to examine the legality of the
impugned order. Besides, any remand at such a belated stage
would only cause further delay in resolution of the dispute between
the parties and would prolong the uncertainty in Tariff
determination. Accordingly, we consider it appropriate to decide the
matter on merits on the basis of the material produced before us by
the parties and within the broader continuum of tariff determination,
so that the controversy is settled in a manner consistent with the
statutory scheme and avoids multiplicity of proceedings.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 19 of 25

27. On the issue of price variation, the Appellant has contended
that there cannot be any price escalation in competitively awarded
packages. A price variation clause is not barred in competitive
bidding contracts. Its permissibility depends on the bid documents
and regulatory framework: if the tender specifies a firm, fixed price,
then escalation is excluded; but if the bidding documents
incorporate a formula-based price variation mechanism, it is legally
valid and enforceable.
28. The Principle of price variation operates as a safeguard
against unforeseen fluctuations in market indices pertaining to
various material, fuel costs, or other input variables that materially
affect the performance of the contract. The mechanism is not
intended to confer windfall gains or shield inefficiencies, but rather
to ensure that the contractual equilibrium envisaged at the time of
bidding is maintained in the face of dynamic economic conditions.
By its very nature, competitive bidding presupposes a fixed and
transparent tariff discovery; however, regulatory frameworks does
not prohibit price variation clause to address volatility in critical
inputs, thereby balancing consumer interest with the viability of the
project. The Respondents, have demonstrated that the contracts
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 20 of 25

entered into by them specifically provided for Price Variation
(PV)/Escalation clauses. During the hearing before this Tribunal,
Respondent No2 has placed a Supply Contract Agreement dated
24.03.2011, which specifically incorporates Price adjustment
provisions and terms and procedure of payments arising therefrom.
We therefore find no merit in the contention of the Appellant that
price variation is impermissible in competitively awarded packages.
29. As regards the date from which price variation applies, it
depends upon the date specified in the bidding documents for the
specific contract, on which all bidders are evaluated. The indices
are applied from that date in the case of the successful bidder’s
contract. It has been submitted by Respondent No. 2, that it has
filed an affidavit dated 24.09.2015 before the Commission, placing
on record the details of price variation including indices and
computational methodology. The amount of price variation in the
indices of various material from March 2010, June 2010 ( One
month prior to bid opening) and October (2012) , the period of major
supplies, as provided by Respondent No 2 has been noted in the
Impugned Oder at paragraph 16 and taking cognizance of such
information, Central Commission has come to finding that increase
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 21 of 25

in the cost is due to the market condition. We therefore find no
merit in the contention of the Appellant that price variation from the
first quarter of 2010 up to October 2012 cannot be applied in the
case of LOA dated 24.03.2011 as well as that the increase in cost
due to price variation cannot be allowed.
30. The increase in cost is also on account of variation in
quantities and reason for such variation is stated to be on account
of difference in quantities of towers and foundation etc. vis- a- vis
the quantities actually used under actual execution as noted in the
submissions of Respondent No 2 in the Impugned Order.
31. It is a settled principle that the quantities indicated in the
Detailed Project Report (DPR) are estimative in nature, prepared
on the basis of preliminary surveys and indicative designs, and
cannot be treated as sacrosanct benchmarks for execution. In the
course of actual implementation, variations in site conditions,
technical requirements, and design refinements inevitably result in
increases or decreases in quantities. In project specific tariff
determination under Section 62 of the Electricity Act, 2003,
increase in quantities cannot be rejected merely on the ground that
they exceed DPR estimates. However prudence check of the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 22 of 25

increase in quantities is required to be undertaken by the
Commission.
32. The central commission has noted the objections filed by
Appellant with regard to increase in cost on account of price
variation and quantity variation, as well as the details provided in
the tariff petition and explanation furnished by Respondent No. 2,
in paragraphs 7 to 12 of the Impugned Order. The Central
Commission after noting the submissions and explanations,
concluded that increase in price was due to actual execution
requirement and market conditions as noted in paragraph 18. This
would indicate that prudence check was undertaken by the Central
commission to arrive at such finding.
33. Appellant has referred to the Performance audit Report No 18
of 2014, of the Controller and Auditor General of India, which was
laid on the table of Parliament House on 04.08.2014, in which it has
been observed that it is desirable that the project is defined to finer
details to the extent possible at the Feasibility Report (FR), Notice
Inviting Tender (NIT) stage for effective planning and scheduling of
the Project. It also suggests that Detailed Survey should be carried
out before the start of procurement process. These observations
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 23 of 25

are advisory in nature and intended for future improvement; These,
in our view, cannot form the basis for denial of cost increase in the
instant case. The Central Commission, in the Impugned order, has
also advised the Respondent No 2, to exercise greater diligence in
future cost estimation.
34. The Appellant has also disputed the approval of Incidental
Expenditure During Constriction of Rs 464.55 Lakh, citing absence
of provision in the 2009-14 Regulations . The Central commission
allowed the said expenditure provisionally considering it to be
within 5 % of hard cost as permitted in other petition and directed
Respondent No 2, to submit year wise details of actual IEDC
discharged till COD at the True Up as noted in Paragraph 21 of the
Impugned Order. This aspect, therefore, stands safeguarded for
subsequent determination.
ORDER
35. In view of the above discussion, we uphold the cost approved
for the subject asset in the impugned order. We, however, advise
the Commission to pass more detailed and reasoned orders in
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 230 of 2016 Page 24 of 25

future, particularly while analyzing cost overruns, so as to obviate
avoidable litigation.
36. The present Appeal is accordingly disposed of in above
terms. All pending IAs, if any, also stand disposed of.
Pronounced in the open court on this 9th day of September, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)

Appeal No. 348 of 2019
31. A short question that arise for our consideration in Appeal No.
348 of 2019 is,
“Whether the ceiling tariff used as a maximum rate for the
purpose of discount in the bid process carried out by
HREDA would also transform itself into the maximum cap
limiting the power of the Commission in the tariff
determination process for the bio-mass generators”.
32. Being mindful about the harmful impact caused by burning of
paddy straw /wheat stubble in the fields and in order to encourage
setting up of paddy straw based biomass power projects in pursuance
to the directions issued by National Green Tribunal, New Delhi,
HREDA issued Request for Proposal (RfP) in the month of August,
2017 inviting proposal for setting up of paddy straw based bio mass
power projects of Build, Own and Operate (BOO) basis in the State
of Haryana through e-tendering process in two bid system i.e.
Technical Bid and Financial Bid. Initially, only six projects of 5MW to
15 MW capacity each were proposed to be set up in the Ambala,
Karnal Kurukshetra, Jind, Kaithal and Fatehabad district of the State
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 15 of 38

on pilot basis such that the total aggregate capacity was about 50
MW.
33. As already noted hereinabove, M/s Jind Bio-Energy & M/s
Fatebhabad Bio-Energy (Appellant Nos. 1 & 2 respectively in Appeal
No. 348 of 2019) through their parent companies namely M/s Jyoti
Renewable Energy Pvt. Limited and M/s Srinivas Sanpla respectively
had submitted their bids in pursuance to the above noted RfP and
were allotted the projects with capacity of 9.9 MW each by the High

34. Clause 1.6 of the RfP relates to the tariff on which the bids were
to be submitted by the prospective bidders and is extracted

the basis of discount offered on the yearly

applicable ceiling tariff approved/notified for the
same by the HERC in the year or their
commissioning. The bidders should make suitable
assumptions and estimations to arrive at such a
projected tariff on their own depending on the

In case, at the time of commissioning of project, the

applicable tariff is not issued by HERC and tariff for

will have to file a petition under Section 62 of the

submission of bids then the generic tariff
notified by the CERC for paddy straw based
power projects for Haryana State shall be taken
as the ceiling tariff and the discount is to be
offered on this tariff only. The bidder with

maximum discount for a district will be selected. In
case of any bidder offering maximum discount in
more than one district, it will be selected for the

further in case of same discount for two districts, the

35. As per clause 1.6.1, the “Ceiling Tariff” applicable shall be the
tariff notified by the Haryana Commission for the year in which the
project is commissioned and in case at the time of commissioning of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 19 of 38

the project, the applicable tariff is not issued by the Haryana
Commission, the tariff for the relevant period as determined by the
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) shall be the
applicable tariff. Thus, the bidders were called upon to make suitable
assumptions to arrive at such projected tariff depending on the
projected year of the Commissioning of their project.
36. The second sentence of this clause 1.6.1. i.e. “the Tariff for sale
of power from such projects under this bidding process will be on the
basis of discount offered on the yearly applicable ceiling tariff
approved/notified for the same by HERC in the year of their
commissioning” clearly indicates that the tariff for sale of power from
bio-mass generators will have to be determined on the basis of
discounts offered by the selected bidders over the generic ceiling tariff
approved by the Commission in the year of the commissioning of
these power projects. It nowhere indicates that the ceiling tariff so
determined by the Commission in the year of commissioning of these
power projects, would be maximum cap for the tariff to be determined
for these power projects during the entire duration of PPA and their
tariff cannot go beyond the ceiling tariff. Manifestly, the generic tariff
approved by the Commission in the year of commissioning of these
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 20 of 38

power projects was relevant only for the purpose of offering discount
by the bidders and the same was not material at the time of
determination of the tariff of these projects by the Commission under
Section 62 of the Electricity Act, 2003 as envisaged under Clause
1.6.2 of the RFP.
37. Clause 1.6.2 provides that the short-listed bidder i.e. the bidder
who emerges successful and to whom power project is allotted, shall
have to approach the Commission for determination of tariff under
Section 62 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and the discounts offered by
that bidder in the bid shall be applicable on such tariff to be fixed by
the Commission for the said project for entire duration of PPA.
38. Thus, the applicability of “Ceiling Tariff” flows from the RfS
document itself which forms the foundational basis of the bidding
process.
39. A conjoint reading of clauses 1.6.1 & 1.6.2 of the RfP envisages
following steps for determination of tariff for a power project allotted
to a successful bidder :-
(a) The bidders had to take into account the annual generic tariff
approved by the Haryana Commission in the year of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 21 of 38

commissioning of the power projects, which was to be
considered as the “Ceiling Tariff”;
(b) The bidders were required to offer the maximum discount on
such generic tariff – ceiling tariff;
(c) In case, generic tariff for paddy straw based projects had not
been issued by the Commission seven days prior to the last
date of submission of bids, the generic tariff notified by the
Central Commission for such power projects for Haryana had
to be taken as ceiling tariff and discount was to be offered on
the same;
(d) The bidders who would offer maximum discount for a district
were to be selected;
(e) The successful bidders were required to approach the
Commission for fixation of tariff for the allocated project under
Section 62 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and the discount offered
by them was to be applicable on such tariff to be fixed by the
Commission for the entire duration of the PPA.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 22 of 38

40. The second sentence of Clause 1.6.2. of the RFP reads as
“consequently the short listed bidder will have to file a petition under
Section 62 of the Electricity Act, 2003 before the Hon’ble HERC for
fixation of tariff for the allocated project and the discount offered shall
be applicable on the tariff fixed by the Hon’ble Commission for the
said project for the entire duration of the PPA” thereby making it
manifest that the discount offered by the bidder at the time of bidding
shall be applicable on the tariff fixed by the Commission for project of
a bidder for the entire duration of the PPA. Therefore, what was to be
applicable throughout the entire duration of the PPA is the “Discount”
offered by the selected bidder and not the “Ceiling Tariff” on which
such discount was offered by the bidder. The language used in this
clause also nowhere indicates that the “Ceiling Tariff” which was to
be considered by the bidders for offering discount while submitting
the bid, would translate into upper cap/limit for the tariff to be
determined by the Commission on yearly basis for such power project
and the tariff so to be determined by the Commission would not go
beyond such cap/limit.
41. Manifestly, a meaningful and purposeful reading of the Clause
1.6.1 & 1.6.2 of the RfP would reveal that no ceiling on the tariff to
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 23 of 38

be determined by the Commission under Section 62 of the Electricity
Act, 2003 for such bio-mass power projects was intended and it was
left to the Commission to determine the tariff for such projects on early
basis without being influenced or without taking into consideration the
“Ceiling Tariff” which was to be taken into account by the bidders
while offering the discounts.
42. The stand taken by HREDA before the Commission as well as
before this Tribunal also supports such interpretation of these clauses
of the RfP. In the reply filed by HREDA to the appeal, it has been
stated as under :
“13. That it is submitted that:
a. The Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) should be as
per the draft PPA attached with the Request for
Proposals (RfP) document, which was approved by the
Hon'ble Commission/HERC.
b. In the projects under consideration in the petition, only
paddy straw is to be used as fuel as per orders of the
HERC and thus variable cost on account of fuel cost is
involved, which cannot be predicted for 20 years at the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 24 of 38

time of preparation of the detailed project
report/proposal. There are many factors like transport,
manpower, demand etc., which may affect the cost of
paddy straw in future and will escalate the variable cost.
c. So, as per the RfP, the tariff for sale of power from such
projects under this bidding process was on the basis of
the discount offered on the yearly applicable tariff to be
approved/notified for the same by the HERC in the year
of their commissioning and accordingly, the Power
Purchase Agreement (PPA) needs to be amended to
make projects viable and successful.”
(Emphasis Supplied)
43. Thus, according to the HREDA also, the bio-mass power
projects would not be viable or successful in case “Ceiling Tariff” is
made applicable during the entire duration of the PPAs. For this
reason, HREDA has stated in the reply that the PPA needs to be
amended in order to make the projects viable and successful. In its
reply filed before the Commission, the HREDA has very clearly stated
as under :-
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 25 of 38

"So, as per the RfP, the tariff for sale of power from such
projects under this bidding process was on the basis of
discount offered on the yearly applicable ceiling tariff
approved /notified for the same by Ld. HERC in the year of
their commissioning, the ceiling tariff of Rs.8 per unit was
mentioned only to select developers on the maximum on
the tariff offered by them."
(Emphasis supplied)
44. Therefore, it is clear beyond any doubt that the “Ceiling Tariff”,
as per the RfP, was applicable only to select the bidders on the
maximum discount on such tariff to be offered by them and the same
was not applicable on the determination of the tariff by the
Commission subsequently, as provided under Clause 1.6.2 of the
RfP.
45. Since the bidding process was initiated by HREDA and the RfP
was also issued by HREDA, its comments with regards to the above
noted clauses of the RfP become very material and cannot be
brushed aside. The principle of “Contemporanea Expositio” i.e.
interpreting a statute or any other document by reference to the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 26 of 38

exposition it has received from contemporary authority, is fully
applicable to the instant case. Therefore, the interpretation sought to
be given by the HREDA to the above noted clauses of the RfP
nevertheless carry considerable weight and is persuasive. In this
regard, we find it apt to rely upon the following paragraph in the
judgement of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Desh Bandhu Gupta &
Co. v. Delhi Stock Exchange Association Ltd., 1979, 4 SCC 565;
9. It may be stated that it was not disputed before us
that these two documents which came into existence
almost simultaneously with the issuance of the notification
could be looked at for finding out the true intention of the
Government in issuing the notification in question,
particularly in regard to the manner in which outstanding
transactions were to be closed or liquidated. The principle
of contemporanea expositio (interpreting a statute or any
other document by reference to the exposition it has
received from contemporary authority) can be invoked
though the same will not always be decisive of the
question of construction (Maxwell 12th ed. P. 268). In
Crawford on Statutory Construction (1940 ed.) in para 219
(at pp. 393-395) it has been stated that administrative
construction (i.e. contemporaneous construction placed
by administrative or executive officers charged with
executing a statute) generally should be clearly wrong
before it is overturned; such a construction, commonly
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 27 of 38

referred to as practical construction, although not
controlling, is nevertheless entitled to considerable
weight; it is highly persuasive. In Baleshwar Bagarli v.
Bhagirathi Dass the principle, which was reiterated in
Mathura Mohan Saha v. Ram Kumar Saha has been stated by
Mookerjee, J. thus:
It is a well-settled principle of interpretation that
courts in construing a statute will give much weight
to the interpretation put upon it, at the time of its
enactment and since, by those whose duty it has
been to construe, execute and apply it… I do not
suggest for a moment that such interpretation has
by any means a controlling effect upon the courts;
such interpretation may, if occasion arises, have to
be disregarded for cogent and persuasive reasons,
and in a clear case of error, a court would without
hesitation refuse to follow such construction.”
46. Similarly, the Hon’ble Supreme Court in another judgement
titled Afcons Infrastructure Limited vs. Nagpur Metro Rail Corporation
Limited & Anr. (2016) 16 SCC 818 has observed on this aspect as
under :-
"15. We may add that the owner or the employer of a
project, having authored the tender documents, is the best
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 28 of 38

person to understand and appreciate its requirements and
interpret its documents. The constitutional courts must
defer to this understanding and appreciation of the tender
documents, unless there is mala fide or perversity in the
understanding or appreciation or in the application of the
terms of the tender conditions . It is possible that the owner
or employer of a project may give an interpretation to the
tender documents that is not acceptable to the
constitutional courts but that by itself is not a reason for
interfering with the interpretation given."
47. In the instant case, we do not find any factual error or legal
infirmity in the interpretation sought to be given by HREDA to the
above noted “RfP” clauses and therefore, we concur with the same.
We do not find any reason to take a different view than what is
canvased by HREDA on the aspect of the applicability of “Ceiling
Tariff”.
48. We may note that the Commission vide its order dated 13th
November, 2025 passed in petition No. 44 of 2025 has fixed the
levelized tariff for M/s Jind Bio-Energy LLP at Rs.9.96 per unit for the
entire life of the project but has applied a ceiling of Rs.8 per unit. The
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 29 of 38

levelized tariff for M/s Fatehabad Bio-Energy LLP has been fixed at
Rs.10.50 per unit by the Commission vide separate order dated 20th
November, 2025 passed in Petition Nos. 45 & 35 for the entire life of
project but the ceiling of Rs.8 per unit has been applied. Therefore, it
is manifest that the Commission itself has determined the tariff which
is higher than the ceiling tariff of Rs.8 per unit which has been applied
to the projects of these two appellants.
49. We may also note that as there was no generic tariff determined
for paddy straw based projects issued by the Haryana Commission,
the bidding was done on the basis of the tariff issued in this regard by
the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission. Accordingly, the
ceiling tariff of Rs.8 per unit was taken from the CERC Renewable
Energy tariff order dated 18th April, 2017 applicable for the Financial
Year 2017-18.
50. In case, the ceiling of Rs.8 per unit is considered as the “Ceiling
Tariff” irrespective of the tariff determined each year by the
Commission under Section 62 of the Electricity Act, 2003 in terms of
Clause 1.6.2 of the RfP, the entire basis of the RfP would be changed
for the reason that the ceiling tariff has been taken from the CERC
order dated 18th April, 2017 which was the basis of bidding at
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 30 of 38

levelized tariff. It needs no mention that the variable cost of
generation of power may vary which has to be considered on actual
basis minus the discount offered by the bidder, without which the
entire project will be unviable. In case the intention was to make the
“Ceiling Tariff”, upon which bidders were supposed to offer discount,
applicable for the entire duration of the PPA then levelized tariff would
have been chosen for offering the discount as opposed to the first
year tariff. We may note that the tariff determined by Central
Commission vide order dated 18th April, 2017 for the Financial Year
2017-18 was chosen for the bid since no other data was available at
the time of bidding. It is evident that none of these projects would
have been commissioned earlier than 24 months from the date of
signing of PPA i.e. in the year 2021-22 and, therefore none of them
would be successful and profitable on the basis of tariff that was
determined five years prior to the date of their commissioning.
51. It was argued on behalf of the HPPC that the tariff framework
based on “Ceiling Tariff” and the discount mechanism as per the RfP
document was accepted by the generators including the Appellants
herein by executing PPAs dated 22nd February, 2019 and, therefore,
once a PPA is executed on the basis of tariff approved by the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 31 of 38

Commission, its terms cannot be re-written to create a new bargain.
The argument has been noted only to be rejected. The PPAs
executed between the Appellants and the HPPC do not specify any
tariff payable by HPPC. Clause 38 of Article 1 of the PPA defines
“Tariff” as the rate payable by the discom as approved by HERC for
every kWh of delivered energy at the metering point. Article 3.3 of the
PPA provides that the seller shall raise invoices on the HPPC for the
energy sold by the seller to HPPC as per the tariff described in Article
2.1.2. As per Article 2.1.2, no additional payment on any account of
whatsoever shall be payable by the HPPC except those approved by
the appropriate Commission/Court of Law. Therefore, whether the
Appellants are entitled to the tariff actually determined by the
Commission under Section 62 of the Electricity Act, 2003 without any
cap/limit of “Ceiling Tariff” upon which discount was offered by them
in the bid process, has to be determined only in terms of the relevant
clauses of the RfP which have been discussed and analyzed
hereinabove. It is manifest that in holding that the cap of “Ceiling
Tariff” would not be applicable on the yearly tariff to be determined by
the Commission under Section 62 of the Electricity Act, 2003 of the
bio-mass power project, we will not be re-writing any new bargain for
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 32 of 38

the parties de hors the provision of the RfP and the same would be
absolutely in consonance with the provisions of the PPA which take
colour from the provisions of the RfP document.
52. Hence, we are unable to countenance the findings of the
Commission in the impugned order that the “Ceiling Tariff” forming
the basis of selection of developers cannot be different than the
ceiling tariff to be considered by the Commission while determination
of tariff for such power projects on the petitions to be filed by
successful bidders. We, therefore, hold that the Commission, while
determining tariff for such projects on yearly basis, cannot apply any
cap/limit and the tariff so determined may go above the “Ceiling Tariff”
on the basis of which discounts were offered by the selected bidders.
Appeal No. 95 of 2022
53. Assail, in this appeal, is to the order dated 15th July, 2019
passed by the Haryana Commission in petition No. 31 of 2019
thereby directing the parties to modify the PPA signed on 22nd
February, 2019.
54. It appears that in the PPA dated 22.02.2019 executed between
the developers and HPPC in pursuance to the order dated 3rd
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 33 of 38

January, 2019 passed in above noted petition No. 25 of 2018, the
definition of “Tariff” was given as under :-
“Tariff” means year to year rate payable by the Discom @
tariff determined by HERC w.r.t. CoD of the project
factoring the discount offered by the IPP as a part of the
RfP for every kW of delivered energy at the metering point
subject to the ceiling tariff i.e. annual generic tariff of
HERC for the year 2017-18 with appropriate factoring of
the discount negotiated with the bidders as a part of the
RfP.”
(Emphasis supplied)
55. In the petition filed by the power generators M/s Jind Bio-
Energy LLP & M/s Fatehabad Bio-Energy LLP, it was contended that
the expression “subject to Ceiling Tariff i.e. annual general tariff of
HERC in the year 2017-18” in the above stated definition of “Tariff”
had been included by HPPC contrary to the order dated 3rd January,
2019 of the Commission passed in case No. 25 of 2018 vide which
the draft PPA was approved by the Commission.
56. Upon comparing the definition of the term “Tariff” in the draft
PPA approved by the Commission vide order dated 3rd January, 2019
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 34 of 38

and in the PPA executed between the parties on 22nd January, 2019,
the Commission observed that HPPC has deviated from the definition
of term “Tariff” as approved in the order dated 3rd January, 2019 and,
therefore, the PPA dated 22nd January, 2019 executed between the
parties is not as per the approved PPA. Accordingly, the Commission
directed the parties to modify the said PPA.
57. It is argued on behalf of the HPPC that the Commission erred
in ignoring that the power generators did not object to said definition
of “Tariff” in the PPA dated 22nd February 2019 at the time of signing
of the PPA duly executed with free-will and consent. Therefore, the
objection raised before the Commission by them to said definition of
term “Tariff” was an after thought. It is submitted that the Commission
has ignored the basic fact that PPA is a contract which has legal
sanctity and unless its terms are held illegal, the same cannot be
reopened by the Commission after the same has been validly
executed between the parties.
58. These arguments are devoid of any substance. It is a settled
legal principle that a PPA becomes effective only upon approval by
the Regulatory Commission even though it may have been signed by
the parties much earlier. Similarly, a PPA executed by the parties
subsequent to the approval of draft PPA by Commission must, in all
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 35 of 38

respects, be in tune with the approved draft PPA. Any deviation
therefrom, even if minor, would render the same otiose and
inapplicable.
59. In the instant case, paragraph 11(ii) of the order dated 3rd
January, 2019 passed by the Commission in Petition No. 45 of 2018
vide which the draft PPA was approved by the Commission is
relevant and is extracted hereinbelow :-
“ii) The Commission has perused the draft PPAs for four
paddy straw based power projects submitted for its
approval. The Commission has noticed a few aberrations
in the same as under:-
a) The definition of Tariff needs to be changed to read that
the tariff payable to the IPP shall be the year to year
tariff determined by the Commission w.r.t. CoD of the
project and the discount offered by the IPPs as part of
the RFP shall be deducted from the year to year tariff
determined by the Commission.”
60. It is, therefore, evident that the Commission, in the said order,
had clearly observed that the tariff payable to the power generators
shall be the year to year tariff determined by the Commission with
respect to COD of the projects and the discount offered by the IPPs
as part of the RfP shall be deducted from the year to year tariff
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 36 of 38

determined by the Commission. Thus, patently, the definition “Tariff”
in the PPAs dated 22nd February, 2019 executed between the parties
is not in consonance with the definition of “Tariff” given in the approval
order dated 3rd January, 2019 of the Commission. The Commission
has rightly observed that in defining the terms “Tariff” in the PPAs
dated 22nd February, 2009, HPPC has deviated from what was
observed and held by the Commission in the PPA approval dated 3rd
January, 2019. Therefore, no error or infirmity can be found in the
impugned order of the Commission directing the parties to modify the
PPA dated 22nd February, 2019 to bring it in tune with the said
approval order.
61. Accordingly, we do not find any merit in the appeal filed by
HPPC.
Conclusion
62. In the light of the above discussion, we allow the Appeal No.
348 of 2019 holding that the Commission, while determining tariff for
the power projects of the Appellants on yearly basis cannot apply any
cap/limit and the tariff so determined may go above the “Ceiling
Tariff” on the basis of which discounts were offered by the selected
bidders. At the same time, we do not find any error or infirmity in the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal Nos. 348 of 2019 & 95 of 2022 Page 37 of 38

order dated 13th July, 2019 passed by the Commission, which has
been impugned in Appeal No. 95 of 2022 and accordingly, said
appeal is hereby dismissed.
Pronounced in the open court on this 9th day of September, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)

PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The appellant, a solar power developer in the State of Karnataka, is
aggrieved by the order dated 11.06.2021 passed by the 1st respondent
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.225 of 2021 Page 2 of 45

Karnataka Electricity Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the
Commission”) in appellant’s petition bearing O.P. No.37/2020 thereby
dismissing the petition wherein the appellant had sought extension of
Scheduled Commercial Operation Date (in short “SCOD”) of its solar power
project on account of force majeure events and a declaration that the
appellant is not liable to bear any liquidated damages as well as reduction in
tariff or any contractual penalty for delay in commissioning of project. The
Commission, in the said impugned order, has held that the case of the
appellant is not covered by the force majeure clause contained in the Power
Purchase Agreement executed by it with the 3rd respondent Bangalore
Electricity Supply Company Limited (in short “BESCOM”) and further held
the appellant entitled to reduced tariff as well as liable to pay liquidated
damages for delay in supply of energy beyond the scheduled commissioning
date in terms of the Power Purchase Agreement.
Description of Parties: -
2. The appellant is a generating company within the meaning of the term
in Section 2(28) of the Electricity Act, 2003 and also is a Special Purpose
Vehicle (in short “SPV”) incorporated by M/s ACME Solar Holdings Private
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.225 of 2021 Page 3 of 45

Limited for setting up of 20MW solar power project in Kudligi Taluka, Bellary
District, Karnataka.
3. The 2nd respondent Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation
Limited (in short “KPTCL”) was incorporated in 1999 upon unbundling of
erstwhile Karnataka Electricity Board with the responsibility of transmission
of power across the State of Karnataka along with
construction/maintenance/development of transmission assets and lines and
other requisite infrastructure for transmission of electricity. It has duly been
granted a transmission license by the Commission vide order dated
06.12.2000 and thus, is discharging the functions of a transmission licensee.
4. The 3rd respondent Bangalore Electricity Supply Company Limited (in
short “BESCOM”) is wholly owned by the Government of Karnataka and is
solely responsible for power distribution in various areas in the State of
Karnataka. The 4th respondent Karnataka Renewable Energy Development
Limited (in short “KREDL”) is an organization working under the purview of
Energy Department, Government of Karnataka with the objective of
promoting renewable energy and to ensure all necessary actions for energy
conservation in the State.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.225 of 2021 Page 4 of 45

Facts and circumstances of the case in brief: -
5. The 4th respondent KREDL had issued a notification dated 07.12.2017
inviting Request for Proposal (RFP) for developing 860 MW grid connected
solar power projects in 43 Talukas in the State of Karnataka, one of them
being Kudligi Taluka. In pursuance to the said notification, KREDL received
proposals from various bidders including the appellant. After evaluation of
the parties, KREDL accepted the bids of the appellant for setting up of solar
power projects in Guledagudda, Kittur, Kudligi and Sidlaghatta Talukas with
the capacity of 15MW, 15MW, 20MW and 20MW respectively. Accordingly,
separate Letters of Award (LOAs) dated 08.02.2018 were issued to the
appellant for setting up of these four power projects. The LOAs were
accepted by the appellant vide letter dated 12.02.2018.
6. In accordance with the RFS notification, the appellant and 2nd
respondent BESCOM entered into Power Purchase Agreements with the
appellant for purchase of power generated from these four solar power
projects. Since we are, in this appeal, concerned with only the 20MW solar
power project of the appellant at Kudligi, we may note that the Power
Purchase Agreement (PPA) dated 22.03.2018 was entered into between
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.225 of 2021 Page 5 of 45

BESCOM and the appellant with respect to the power to be generated in the
said solar power project to be set up at Kudligi.
7. Subsequent to the signing of the PPA, the appellant applied for
connectivity of the project to 220/66kV Kudligi sub-station on 02.05.2018.
8. The PPA dated 22.03.2018 executed between the parties received
approval from the Commission on 04.05.2018. Since Article 3.1 of the PPA
provided that the “effective date” on which the agreement shall come into
effect will be the date of getting concurrence from KERC, the appellant was
required to achieve commercial operation of the power project within 18
months from 04.05.2018 i.e. the date when the PPA was approved by the
Commission. Therefore, the SCOD of the project was 03.11.2019. The 2nd
respondent KPTCL issued tentative evacuation scheme approval to the
appellant on 06.10.2018 which was accepted by the appellant vide letter
dated 09.10.2018. Thereafter, KPTCL issued regular evacuation scheme for
the proposed 220MW solar power project at Kudligi on 19.11.2018.
9. Since the appellant sensed delay in the completion of 220/66kV Kudligi
sub-station as well as upstream transmission line, through which it had to
evacuate power, it addressed a letter dated 07.02.2019 to the General
Manager, BESCOM, conveying that any delay in completion of line being
constructed on the upstream of Kudligi sub-station, would have impact on
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.225 of 2021 Page 6 of 45

the commissioning schedule of the power project as envisaged under the
PPA and further, upon invoking Article 14.3.1 of the PPA (force majeure
clause), the appellant requested BESCOM for appropriate extension of time
for commissioning of the power project equivalent to such delay. Vide letter
dated 11.03.2019, the appellant reiterated the assertions made in previous
letter dated 07.02.2019 and requested KPTCL to furnish the present status
and definitive timeline for completion as well as commissioning of 220/66kV
Kudligi sub-station and upstream transmission lines from the same within
seven days of the receipt of the letter.
10. In its response dated 21.03.2019 to the appellant’s communication
dated 11.03.2019, KPTCL gave the probable date of commissioning of
220kV Kudligi sub-station as 30.04.2019 and that of incoming line & terminal
bay as 30.06.2019.
11. The appellant, vide letter dated 12.07.2019, again requested KPTCL
to confirm the present status of commissioning of 220kV Kudligi sub-station
as well as 220kV Kudligi upstream transmission line. Similar request was
made by appellant in the subsequent two letters dated 29.08.2019 and
31.08.2019.
12. It appears that since no such confirmation was received by the
appellant from KPTCL, it filed a petition before the Commission seeking
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.225 of 2021 Page 7 of 45

directions to KPTCL to commission the Kudligi sub-station at the earliest.
Some other reliefs were also claimed in the petition. However, the petition
was withdrawn by the appellant on 31.12.2019 with liberty to approach the
Commission after the commissioning of Kudligi sub-station and its own
power project. Vide letter dated 30.09.2019, BESCOM reminded the
appellant that in view of the provisions of the RFP, it was the responsibility
of the project developer i.e. the appellant to obtain power evacuation
approval for the power project to the nearest sub-station/delivery point as
mentioned in the PPA, and accordingly, appellant was advised to approach
KPTCL to obtain clarification regarding the present status of commissioning
of 220kV Kudligi sub-station as well as 220kV Kudligi upstream transmission
line.
13. The appellant contends that as per the suggestion of BESCOM, it
again approached KPTCL and was informed that Kudligi sub-station will not
be available for evacuation of power by the SCOD of the appellant’s power
project i.e. 03.11.2019.
14. Thereafter, the appellant issued force majeure notice dated
23.10.2019 to the BESCOM saying that the power project of the appellant
could not be commissioned on account of delay on the part of KPTCL in
commissioning the Kudligi sub-station as well as upstream transmission line
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.225 of 2021 Page 8 of 45

thereby affecting its performance under the PPA. Accordingly, request was
made to provide extension of the SCOD of the power project in view of the
said force majeure event and not to take any coercive action against the
appellant.
15. On the same very day i.e. 23.10.2019, Chief Electrical Inspectorate to
the Government of Karnataka issued approval of electrical installations in the
power project of the appellant (CEIG approval). PTCC approval was also
issued by the Divisional Engineer, Telecom, Power Telecommunication
Coordination Committee on the same day i.e. 23.10.2019.
16. In pursuance to the said CEIG approval, appellant applied for regular
interconnection approval to KPTCL vide letter dated 28.10.2019 for
interconnecting the solar power plant with 220kV Kudligi sub-station so that
the power project may be commissioned. KPTCL responded to the same on
06.01.2020 stating that 66kV terminal bay work was pending at both
220/66kV Kudligi sub-station end and at the end of power project. The
appellant was asked to complete the same. Vide letter dated 29.01.2020.
appellant informed KPTCL that all such work within its scope was already
competed and only cable termination at Kudligi sub-station was pending due
to various reasons which included lack of support from KPTCL officials.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.225 of 2021 Page 9 of 45

17. Vide subsequent letters dated 13.02.2020 and 19.02.2020, appellant
requested KPTCL to take immediate steps to complete and charge 220kV
Kudligi sub-station and also sought support of its officials for the pre-
commissioning testing of the power project. Since, the appellant appears to
have not received any response from KPTCL, it wrote to the State
Government on 26.02.2020 with the request to intervene and advise KPTCL
to take immediate steps to charge the said Kudligi sub-station and to extend
requisite support to the appellant for conducting the pre-commissioning
testing.
18. Thereafter, the appellant received letter dated 12.03.2020 from KPTCL
stating that a few activities at bay end of the Kudligi sub-station are pending
and also sought certain documents from the appellant for consideration of its
request of interconnection approval. This was responded to by the appellant
vide letter dated 17.03.2020.
19. It appears that some progress was made in the work at the end of
KPTCL for charging 220kV Kudligi sub-station but the work was again put on
hold due to countrywide lockdown on account of spread of Covid-19.
20. Ultimately, Electrical Inspectorate, Government of Karnataka provided
provisional approval for electrical installations pertaining to 220kV DC line
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.225 of 2021 Page 10 of 45

from existing 400/220kV Jagalur KPTCL sub-station to existing 220/66kV
Kudligi sub-station on 20.04.2020. On the same day, Electrical Inspectorate
also provided provisional approval for electrical installation pertaining to
220/66kV Kudligi sub-station.
21. In pursuance to these approvals, the EPC contractor of KPTCL
consented to charge the 220/66kV Kudligi sub-station. Thereafter, requisite
pre-commissioning test for Kudligi sub-station was carried on from
27.05.2020 to 30.05.2020 and the same was test charged on 30.05.2020 at
5:31 P.M.
22. Commissioning certificate for the solar power project in question was
issued by KPTCL to the appellant on 02.06.2020 declaring the same as
commissioned and interconnected to KPTCL Grid situated at 220/66kV
Kudligi on 30.05.2020 at 1900 Hrs. Thus, the 20MW solar power project of
the appellant achieved Commercial Operation (Commercial Operation Date)
on 30.05.2020.
23. In view of these facts and circumstances, the appellant filed petition
no.37/2020 before the Commission seeking extension of SCOD of the power
project from 03.11.2019 to 30.05.2020 on account of force majeure events
not attributable to the appellant and a declaration that the appellant will not
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.225 of 2021 Page 11 of 45

be liable to bear any liquidated damages, reduced tariff and other contractual
penalties for delay in commissioning of the project. The petition has been
dismissed by the Commission vide impugned order dated 11.06.2021
thereby denying all the reliefs sought by the appellant.
24. Accordingly, the appellant is before us in this appeal challenging the
observations and findings of the Commission in the impugned order.
Findings of the Commission in the impugned order: -
25. We may note that the Commission had framed following eight issues
for its consideration: -
“Issue No.1: Whether on or before the Scheduled Commissioning
Date (SCD), construction works of the Solar Power
Project of the Petitioner was completed and the said
Project was ready for commissioning?
Issue No.2: If Issue No.1 is held in negative, on which date the
Solar Power Project was ready for commissioning?
Issue No.3: Whether in the facts and circumstances of the present
case, the acceptance of conditional evacuation scheme
approval by the Petitioner precludes it from claiming any
relief under Force Majeure event for the period during
which the evacuation system of 2nd Respondent
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.225 of 2021 Page 12 of 45

(KPTCL) was not made available for evacuation of
power from the Solar Power Project?
Issue No.4: Whether in the facts and circumstances of present
case, the Petitioner had the obligation to go for
alternative methods of evacuation of power?
Issue No.5: Whether delay in commissioning of Kudligi Sub-
station would fall under the definition of Force Majeure
as per Article 14 of the PPA?
Issue No.6: Whether the 1st Respondent (BESCOM) is entitled to
claim Liquidated Damages at the rates specified in
Article 5.8 of the PPA?
Issue No.7: To which reliefs the parties are entitled to?
Issue No.8: What Order?”
26. issue no.1 has been decided in appellant’s favour. The Commission
has held that the appellant had completed the construction works of the solar
power project well before its SCOD i.e. 03.11.2019 and accordingly did not
find it necessary to return any findings on issue no.2.
27. On issue no.3, the Commission has opined that the appellant is
precluded from invoking the force majeure clause of the PPA and its case

consent, approval or permit.”
53. The words “permit”, “authorization” and “consent” used in this clause
of the PPA are material in the context of the present case. The appellant
could not have commissioned its power project, even though it was ready for
commissioning by the SCOD, unless it got permission or authorization or
consent from KPTCL which was to be given as soon as the KPTCL
completed and commissioned the Kudligi sub-station as well as the
upstream transmission line. Since no such permission/authorization/consent
came from KPTCL on account of delay in completion/commissioning of the
said sub-station as well as transmission line beyond the SCOD of the
appellant’s power project, the same qualifies as a force majeure event which
was undoubtedly beyond the control of the appellant and could not have
been presaged by the appellant in view of the correspondences exchanged
between appellant and KPTCL, as discussed hereinabove. Further, KPTCL,
being a government controlled company, the appellant does not have any
control over its functioning. The appellant could, at best, pursue KPTCL to

expedite the completion/commissioning of the said sub-station as well as
transmission line which it did but still these two assets could not be
commissioned by or before the SCOD of appellant’s power project. The
delay in completion/commissioning of these two assets is attributable solely
to the KPTCL for which appellant cannot be held responsible.
54. Further, even otherwise also, we are of the opinion that even if
KPTCL’s event of default is not specifically stated in the PPA as a ground for
extension in favour of the project developer, the same can be read into the
PPA in order to lend business efficacy to the provision of the PPA. We are
conscious of the fact that this Tribunal cannot add anything to the terms of a
PPA which has duly been agreed to as well as signed between the parties
and also approved by the regulatory Commission. However, the terms of the
PPA be construed in a way which advances the rights and interests of both
the parties and does not put any of the parties in any detrimental or
prejudicial situation for which the affected party is not to blame.
55. On this aspect, we find it relevant to refer to the judgment of the Hon’ble
Supreme Court in Nabha Power Limited v. Punjab State Power Corporation
Limited (2018) 11 SCC 508, wherein the apex court had the occasion to
interpret the terms of the commercial contract by looking inter alia into the

definition clause and has laid down guiding principles on how the terms of
commercial contracts should be interpreted. It has been held: -
“It should certainly not be an endeavour of commercial
courts to look to implied terms of contract. In the current
day and age, making of contracts is a matter of high
technical expertise with legal brains from all sides
involved in the process of drafting a contract. It is even
preceded by opportunities of seeking clarifications and
doubts so that the parties know what they are getting
into. Thus, normally a contract should be read as it
reads, as per its express terms. The implied terms is a
concept, which is necessitated only when the Penta-test
referred to aforesaid comes into play. There has to be a
strict necessity for it.”
56. The “Penta-test” as referred by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the
above judgment to ascertain implied terms while interpreting commercial
contracts is as under: -
“(1) it must be reasonable and equitable;
(2) it must be necessary to give business efficacy to the
contract, so that no term will be implied if the contract is
effective without it;
(3) it must be so obvious that "it goes without saying";
(4) it must be capable of clear expression;
(5) it must not contradict any express term of the
contract.”
